passage.title: The Whisper Under the Millstone
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Passage
passage.text:
Late July heat baked the red clay hills of North Carolina. Yet a cool breath of mist drifted from the stone foundation of the old Hawkins gristmill. Eleven-year-old Eli and his sister Nora stood beside the giant wooden waterwheel, which had not turned a single inch in forty years. The surface creek above the dam was parched and cracked from a month without rain. Even so, Eli could hear a faint, steady gurgle somewhere deep beneath the mossy granite blocks.

Nora knelt by the dry wooden chute that once fed the wheel. She shone her flashlight along the stone wall where an iron grate sat half buried in leaves. Their grandfather had told them that the mill builder had tapped a cold mountain spring to keep grain grinding during summer droughts. Over the decades, however, the hidden channel had vanished from sight. Beneath the mossy oak beams of the dry millrace, the hidden stone arch of the old springhouse was completely blocked by fallen slate and tangled hemlock roots.

Eli stepped into the cool trench and pressed his palm against the damp slate slabs. The rock felt icy against his skin, proving that subterranean water was still pooling right behind the wall. If they pried all the heavy stones out at once, a sudden surge of mud might flood the lower cellar of the mill. Instead, Nora pointed to a narrow weep hole at the base of the arch where a thin ribbon of clear water trickled out.

Working with a flat iron pry bar and a cedar branch, the two explorers cleared the lower outlet first. Eli braced his boots against the granite sill and dislodged a wedge of gray slate near the bottom corner. Right away, a stream of cold, clear spring water gushed into the stone trough, washing away decades of dark silt. As the pressure behind the wall dropped, they lifted the tangled hemlock roots out of the arch without a slide.

Inside the low stone chamber, two clear limestone streams converged in a deep basin carved out of solid bedrock. The water was so pure that Eli could count the white quartz pebbles resting on the bottom. Following the stone gutter they had just cleared, the spring flowed down the chute and dripped onto the lower blades of the great wheel. With a deep groan of seasoned oak, the old waterwheel shifted an inch, keeping the builder's secret promise alive.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 2:

"Beneath the mossy oak beams of the dry millrace, the hidden stone arch of the old springhouse was completely blocked by fallen slate and tangled hemlock roots."

Based on the structure of this sentence, what actually blocked the stone arch of the springhouse?

options.text: The mossy oak beams of the dry millrace
options.childFeedback: 'Beneath the mossy oak beams of the dry millrace' only tells WHERE the stone arch sat—the oak beams above didn't block the arch!

options.text: The hidden stone arch pressing down on the creek
options.childFeedback: The hidden stone arch is what got blocked ('was completely blocked')—it didn't press down on the creek or block itself!

options.text: Fallen slate and tangled hemlock roots
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 2, the passive verb 'was completely blocked by' tells us that 'fallen slate and tangled hemlock roots' are what blocked the hidden stone arch of the old springhouse.

options.text: Bags of grain left inside the lower cellar by the miller
options.childFeedback: The mill hadn't turned in forty years, and no bags of grain are mentioned in Paragraph 2; fallen slate and hemlock roots blocked the arch.

questions.provingSentenceText: Beneath the mossy oak beams of the dry millrace, the hidden stone arch of the old springhouse was completely blocked by fallen slate and tangled hemlock roots.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 2, the passive verb 'was completely blocked by' tells us that 'fallen slate and tangled hemlock roots' are what blocked the hidden stone arch of the old springhouse.
questions.parentExplanation: Aligned to ELAGSE5L1, this passive sentence begins with a prepositional phrase and places the receiver ('the hidden stone arch') before the verb. The true grammatical actor appears after 'by': 'fallen slate and tangled hemlock roots' (Option C).
questions.retryHint: Look right after 'was completely blocked by' in Paragraph 2 to see what blocked the stone arch.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 3:

"The rock felt icy against his skin, proving that subterranean water was still pooling right behind the wall."

What does the word "subterranean" mean as it is used in this sentence?

options.text: Flowing or located beneath the surface of the ground
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 3, 'subterranean' means flowing or located beneath the surface of the ground. The icy rock proved that underground spring water was still pooling behind the buried stone wall.

options.text: Heated by the July sun on top of the red clay hills
options.childFeedback: Heated by the July sun on top of the hills is the exact opposite! Paragraph 3 says the slate felt icy because the water was deep underground.

options.text: Poured from a plastic water bottle carried in a backpack
options.childFeedback: Eli and Nora aren't pouring water from a backpack bottle; they are feeling icy spring water pooling naturally behind the underground stone wall.

options.text: Frozen into solid blocks of winter ice all year long
options.childFeedback: The spring water feels icy-cold in July, but it is liquid water that gushes out in Paragraph 4—not frozen into solid blocks of ice all year!

questions.provingSentenceText: The rock felt icy against his skin, proving that subterranean water was still pooling right behind the wall.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 3, 'subterranean' means flowing or located beneath the surface of the ground. The icy rock proved that underground spring water was still pooling behind the buried stone wall.
questions.parentExplanation: From Latin 'sub-' (under) and 'terra' (earth), 'subterranean' describes the hidden underground spring water pooling behind the buried stone wall (Option A).
questions.retryHint: Break 'subterranean' into its parts—'sub' (under) and 'terra' (earth or ground)—and think about where the hidden spring water is pooling.

questions.prompt: Why do Eli and Nora clear the narrow weep hole at the bottom of the arch before removing all the heavy stones?

options.text: They want to keep the spring water locked inside the cave so the waterwheel never turns.
options.childFeedback: Eli and Nora want to free the spring water so it flows down the chute, not lock it inside! In Paragraph 5, their work makes the old waterwheel shift again.

options.text: They hope to trap white quartz pebbles inside the iron grate to sell in town.
options.childFeedback: They aren't trying to trap quartz pebbles to sell in town; Paragraph 5 only mentions the white pebbles to show how clear the spring water is.

options.text: They are afraid the cedar branch will snap if it touches the mossy oak beams.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 4, they use the cedar branch and iron pry bar to clear the lower outlet—they aren't worried about the branch touching the oak beams.

options.text: They want to let the water pressure drop safely so a sudden mud surge does not flood the mill cellar.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 3 explains that prying all the heavy stones out at once could unleash a mud surge into the mill cellar, so clearing the small weep hole first lets the water pressure drop safely.

questions.provingSentenceText: If they pried all the heavy stones out at once, a sudden surge of mud might flood the lower cellar of the mill.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 3 explains that prying all the heavy stones out at once could unleash a mud surge into the mill cellar, so clearing the small weep hole first lets the water pressure drop safely.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 3 explains that prying out all the stones at once could unleash a sudden surge of mud into the lower cellar; releasing the water gradually through the lower outlet drops the pressure safely first (Option A).
questions.retryHint: Check the third sentence of Paragraph 3 to see what danger would happen if they pried out all the heavy stones at once.

questions.prompt:
Read these sentences from Paragraph 1:

"The surface creek above the dam was parched and cracked from a month without rain. Even so, Eli could hear a faint, steady gurgle somewhere deep beneath the mossy granite blocks."

How does the transition phrase "Even so" connect these two sentences?

options.text: It shows that the dry weather caused the granite blocks to crack in half.
options.childFeedback: It was the red clay surface creek bed that was parched and cracked from drought in Paragraph 1, not the mossy granite blocks!

options.text: It introduces a surprising contrast between the bone-dry surface creek and the hidden water still flowing underground.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 1, the transition phrase 'Even so' works like 'Despite that' to show a surprising contrast: even though the surface creek is bone-dry from drought, Eli still hears water gurgling underground.

options.text: It proves that Eli was imagining the sound of water because no water existed anywhere near the mill.
options.childFeedback: Eli isn't imagining the sound at all! In Paragraphs 3 through 5, he and Nora uncover the real underground spring gurgling behind the wall.

options.text: It explains the exact year when the Hawkins family built the wooden dam.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 1 says the waterwheel hadn't turned in forty years, but 'Even so' introduces the sound of hidden water, not the year the dam was built.

questions.provingSentenceText: Even so, Eli could hear a faint, steady gurgle somewhere deep beneath the mossy granite blocks.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 1, the transition phrase 'Even so' works like 'Despite that' to show a surprising contrast: even though the surface creek is bone-dry from drought, Eli still hears water gurgling underground.
questions.parentExplanation: Aligned to ELAGSE5L1, the conjunctive phrase 'Even so' signals a concession/contrast: despite the surface creek being parched from drought, Eli still hears water gurgling underground (Option B).
questions.retryHint: Compare the two sentences in Paragraph 1: the surface creek is dry and cracked, yet what does Eli hear right after 'Even so'?

questions.prompt: PART A: What mystery from their grandfather's story do Eli and Nora confirm by the end of the passage?

options.text: The giant oak waterwheel was too heavy to ever move again without an electric motor.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 5 proves the waterwheel CAN still move without an electric motor: as soon as the spring water drips onto the blades, the oak wheel shifts an inch!

options.text: The old miller had hidden bags of gold coins beneath the white quartz pebbles in the basin.
options.childFeedback: There are no bags of gold coins under the pebbles! The 'builder's secret promise' in Paragraph 5 is the hidden mountain spring that keeps water flowing during droughts.

options.text: The mill builder had connected a hidden underground spring to the chute so the mill could run even during summer droughts.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 2, the children recall their grandfather's story that the mill builder tapped a mountain spring for summer droughts, and clearing the blocked arch in Paragraphs 4 and 5 proves it when the waterwheel shifts.

options.text: Hemlock trees only grow inside dark stone caves where no sunlight can reach.
options.childFeedback: Hemlock roots had tangled in the shady millrace trench outside (Paragraph 2), not grown as full trees inside a dark cave without sunlight!

questions.provingSentenceText: Their grandfather had told them that the mill builder had tapped a cold mountain spring to keep grain grinding during summer droughts.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 2, the children recall their grandfather's story that the mill builder tapped a mountain spring for summer droughts, and clearing the blocked arch in Paragraphs 4 and 5 proves it when the waterwheel shifts.
questions.parentExplanation: In Paragraph 2, the children recall their grandfather's account that the mill builder tapped a mountain spring for summer droughts; by clearing the blocked arch in Paragraphs 4–5, they confirm the hidden springhouse and watch its water shift the wheel (Option A).
questions.retryHint: Connect what their grandfather told them in Paragraph 2 with what happens when the cleared spring water reaches the wheel in Paragraph 5.

questions.prompt: PART B: Which quotation from the passage best supports the correct answer to Question 5?

options.text: "Their grandfather had told them that the mill builder had tapped a cold mountain spring to keep grain grinding during summer droughts."
options.childFeedback: This sentence from Paragraph 2 directly supports Question 5 by stating the grandfather's story about the hidden drought-proof mountain spring that Eli and Nora uncover.

options.text: "Late July heat baked the red clay hills of North Carolina."
options.childFeedback: This opening line from Paragraph 1 only describes the hot July weather in North Carolina, not the grandfather's story about the hidden spring.

options.text: "Working with a flat iron pry bar and a cedar branch, the two explorers cleared the lower outlet first."
options.childFeedback: This sentence from Paragraph 4 shows the tools Eli and Nora used to clear the stones, without stating the mystery from their grandfather's story.

options.text: "The water was so pure that Eli could count the white quartz pebbles resting on the bottom."
options.childFeedback: This detail from Paragraph 5 only shows how clear the water was in the basin, not why the mill builder tapped the spring for summer droughts.

questions.provingSentenceText: Their grandfather had told them that the mill builder had tapped a cold mountain spring to keep grain grinding during summer droughts.
questions.childTip: This sentence from Paragraph 2 directly supports Question 5 by stating the grandfather's story about the hidden drought-proof mountain spring that Eli and Nora uncover.
questions.parentExplanation: Option B directly states the grandfather's story about the drought-proof mountain spring that Eli and Nora uncover and verify by the end of the passage.
questions.retryHint: Check Paragraph 2 for the sentence about what their grandfather told them the mill builder had tapped for summer droughts.
